## Paper

## Abstract

Ciliopathies are genetic disorders characterized by defective primary cilia function, with obesity as a clinical manifestation in certain cases, including Alström syndrome, which is caused by ALMS1 mutations. The link between cilia and lipid metabolism remains poorly understood, but evidence suggests a role for impaired autophagy. Autophagy affects both intra- and extracellular levels of ACBP, which can act as an obesogenic factor. Our multi-omics study reveals early hepatic dyslipidemia, impaired autophagy, and hepatic accumulation of ACBP in presymptomatic male mice lacking Alms1 gene. These conditions are consistent with the obesogenic phenotype and with alterations in the gut microbiota that manifest as the mice age and develop obesity. Importantly, reducing excessive ACBP with a neutralizing monoclonal antibody limits weight gain and metabolic defects in Alms1-/- mice in an autophagy-independent manner. Altogether, the data support the idea that ciliopathy-associated obesity, particularly Alström syndrome, may be mitigated by ACBP neutralization.

---

## Introduction

The primary cilium is an elongated cellular organelle consisting of a membrane-enclosed axoneme composed of microtubules and a basal body derived from a centriole that plays a key role in regulating diverse cellular processes including metabolism1,2. Defects in cilia function trigger a group of disorders known as ciliopathies3. One of these diseases is Alström syndrome (AöS), a rare autosomal recessive and pleiotropic disorder, caused by mutations in the ALMS1 gene4. AöS presents metabolic problems, such as insulin resistance, diabetes, obesity, and liver abnormalities5–8, and non-metabolic symptoms, such as sensorineural hearing loss, retinal degeneration and cardiomyopathy leading to heart failure. Most current treatments for AöS primarily focus on palliative care, addressing individual symptoms without actually curing or preventing the disease9.

The mechanisms by which obesity may be related to ciliary dysfunction remain unclear, but recent research suggests a potential link through impaired autophagy. Autophagy is an evolutionarily conserved catabolic process that allows cells to eliminatedysfunctional components by sequestering them within double-membrane autophagosomes10–13. Ciliogenesis and autophagy are both activated during nutritional deprivation, and both are necessary for the maintenance of bioenergetic homeostasis14,15. In addition, ciliogenesis and autophagy exhibit bidirectional functional connections. The cilium-dependent signaling is necessary for the formation of the autophagosome through the recruitment of proteins related to autophagy. Conversely, autophagy regulates both ciliogenesis and the length of the cilium through the degradation of specific proteins involved in the formation of cilia15–18. Moreover, autophagy functions as a survival mechanism that allows cells to adapt to environmental changes and contributes to cellular health by the selective removal and recycling of damaged cellular components. Autophagy also contributes to pathogens defense and atypical protein secretion, concerning factors like interleukin-1, interleukin-6 and acyl-CoA binding protein (ACBP)19–22. This wide range of cellular functions makes the maintenance of cellular homeostasis, both under physiological and pathological conditions, closely dependent on the autophagic capacity23. Thus, the cell responds to alterations in the extracellular and intracellular environment by adjusting the autophagic flux in response to internal metabolic demands, thereby contributing to stress adaptation, organismal homeostasis and healthy ageing12. In fact, several genetic or pharmacological autophagy activation confer improvements in health and lifespan to model organisms, including yeast, nematodes, flies and mice24. Conversely, deficient autophagy contributes to the development of major human diseases, including neurodegenerative and cardiovascular diseases, carcinogenesis and metabolic syndrome25,26. Prolonged genetic or pharmacological autophagy inhibition promotes an obesogenic phenotype and compromises weight loss during fasting.

ACBP has emerged as a novel lipogenic factor that is altered in obesity20, and anorexia27. Studies in animal models and cell cultures demonstrated that acute nutrient deprivation and autophagic activation led to ACBP secretion, reducing intracellular ACBP and increasing extracellular ACBP. Pharmacological ACBP reduction with neutralizing antibodies mimics the effects of a low-calorie diet or increased physical activity, enhancing lipolysis, and causing temporary hyperglycemia, which inhibits food intake. Conversely, systemic administration of recombinant ACBP results in temporary hypoglycemia as glucose is redirected for lipid synthesis, increasing appetite20,28–33. In fact, it has recently been described that supplementation with extracellular ACBP might constitute a viable strategy for treating anorexia nervosa and chemotherapy-induced cachexia27.

Our research aims to investigate the interplay between primary cilia, autophagy, and ACBP in AöS. As shown here, we observed that the ALMS1 mutation in mice caused a systemic autophagy defect coupled to increased ACBP levels. Neutralization of ACBP fully prevented the development of obesity, arguing in favor of a pathogenic role of ACBP in AöS.

---

## Results

Asymptomatic Alms1-/- mice: early metabolic alterations
To characterize the metabolic events occurring in mice both prior to (Fig. 1) and after the onset of obesity associated with AöS (Fig. 2), we conducted metabolomic analyses of the liver, white adipose tissue (WAT), and plasma, and transcriptomic analyses of the liver, from Alms1 deficient (Alms1-/-) mice, which express a truncated protein without any residual function (Fig. 1a). As previously described34, no changes in body weight were observed between Alms1 wild-type (WT) and Alms1-/- mice up to 8 weeks of age. However, at a later stage, these strains of mice gradually diverged in their body weight, and Alms1-/- mice developed hyperglycemia (Fig. 1b, c). To unravel the metabolic modifications associated with the onset of obesity and diabetes, we conducted metabolomic and transcriptomic analyses on WT and Alms1-/- mice at three distinct ages: at 6 weeks of age (before the development of AöS symptoms), at 10 weeks of age (when Alms1-/- mice have acquired initial signs of an AöS-like phenotype, including obesity), and at 20 weeks of age (when Alms1-/- mice have developed an advanced AöS-like phenotype) (Fig. 1d).

We compared the metabolome of 6-week-old WT and Alms1-/- mice, which are indistinguishable with respect to their body weight and blood glucose levels (Supplementary Fig. 1a–c). At this early, pre-obese stage, differential enrichment metabolomic analysis identified metabolic alterations primarily in the liver (Fig. 1e, f and Supplementary Data 1), with 77 metabolites dysregulated due to the Alms1 mutation. In the plasma, Alms1-/- mice exhibited a selective reduction of one single metabolite, N-acetyl-DL-tryptophan (Supplementary Fig. 1d and Supplementary Data 1). In WAT, young Alms1-/- mice manifested a significant reduction in two metabolites, spermine and prostaglandin E1 (Supplementary Fig. 1e and Supplementary Data 1). Livers from Alms1-/- mice exhibited impaired lipid metabolism, marked by significant reductions in acylcarnitines, free fatty acids, and phosphatidylcholines (Fig. 1f). Additional alterations were observed in various pathways involving linoleic and linolenic acids, specifically phosphatidylethanolamine biosynthesis, as well as the transport of acyl groups into mitochondria, among others (Supplementary Fig. 1f–h). These findings highlight the liver’s central role in AöS pathogenesis. Consequently, we performed transcriptomic analyses of livers from 6-week-old WT and Alms1-/- mice (Fig. 1g–h and Supplementary Data 2), revealing alterations in the expression of 19 hepatic genes, highlighting genes related to metabolic stress, inflammation, and the regulation of protein synthesis.

Transcriptome and metabolome analysis in obese Alms1-/- mice
Next, we compared the metabolic profiles of early obese 10-week-old Alms1-/- mice with those of WT mice with diet-induced obesity (DIO) (Supplementary Fig. 2a and Supplementary Data 3). As expected, most of the metabolic alterations overlapped among both models of obesity (Fig. 2a, b and Supplementary Fig. 2b), suggesting that they cannot be attributed to specific effects of the Alms1 mutation itself. Therefore, we focused on metabolites that were modulated in Alms1-/- mice only, not by DIO (Fig. 2c). Alms1-/- mice, but not DIO mice, exhibited the accumulation of glucuronic and succinic acid, as well as increased C6:0 and C5:0 carnitines (red square in Fig. 2c). We also observed, among other changes, a decrease in phosphatidylcholine (17:0) and retinoic acid in Alms1-/- mice, but not in DIO mice (blue square in Fig. 2c), indicating an Alms1 mutation-dependent mitochondrial dysfunction and alterations in fatty acid β-oxidation.

Finally, as compared to their WT controls, 20-week-old AöS Alms1-/- mice were markedly overweight and hyperglycemic (Supplementary Fig. 2c–e) and exhibited numerous differences in their mass spectrometric metabolomics profile (Supplementary Data 4) that affected plasma (Supplementary Fig. 2f), WAT (Supplementary Fig. 2g) and liver (Fig. 2d, e and Supplementary Fig. 2h). In addition, 20-week-old AöS Alms1-/- mice exhibited numerous changes in gene expression in the liver (Fig. 2f, g and Supplementary Data 5). These changes concerned multiple biochemical pathways, including lipid, carbohydrate and protein metabolism, suggesting a rather widespread metabolic perturbation in advanced AöS.

Disabled autophagy and elevated ACBP levels in AöS
Next, we examined the hepatic genes and proteins associated with lipid metabolism from pre-syndromic (6-week-old) and syndromic (20-week-old) Alms1-/- mice (Fig. 3 and Supplementary Fig. 3). Consistent with the results observed in the transcriptomic analyses (Supplementary Data 2 and 5), livers from 6-week-old Alms1-/- mice revealed no significant changes in mRNAs related to lipogenesis, including fatty acid synthase (Fasn), peroxisome proliferator-activated receptor gamma (Pparg), acetyl-CoA carboxylase 1 (Acc1), sterol regulatory element binding protein (Srebp1) and Acbp, or related to lipolysis, as AMP-activated protein kinase (Ampk) and carnitine palmitoyltransferase 1 (Cpt1). However, livers from 6-week-old Alms1-/- mice exhibited an important reduction in mRNAs coding for peroxisome proliferator-activated receptor gamma coactivator 1 (Pgc1), adipose triglyceride lipase (AtgL) mRNAs (Supplementary Fig. 3a). In 20-week-old Alms1-/- mice several lipogenesis genes (Acc1, Cpt1, Fasn, Srebp1 or Pparg) were upregulated, but hepatic Acbp mRNA levels remained stable (Supplementary Fig. 3b). This contrasted with the observation that ACBP protein was elevated in both 6- and 20-week-old Alms1-/- mice compared to WT mice (Fig. 3a, b). We therefore measured autophagy, which is known to affect intracellular ACBP protein levels at the post-transcriptional level. We observed a significant increase in the autophagy substrate sequestosome 1 (SQSTM1, best known as p62) levels in both 6- and 20-week-old Alms1-/- mice, as compared to age-matched WT controls, suggesting a reduction in autophagic flux (Fig. 3a, c). The ratio of lipidated over non-lipidated microtubule-associated protein light chain 3 (LC3-II/LC3-I) (Fig. 3a, d), was not changed at younger but increased in adult mice. These results suggest that autophagy is blocked through different steps: (i) early, before autophagosome formation at 6 weeks of age (Fig. 3a–d), corroborated with an autophagic flux inhibitor, such as leupeptin, that effectively increases ACBP and SQSTM1 levels (Fig. 3e–f and Supplementary Fig. 3c) and showed a decrease in the degradation flux (Fig. 3g); (ii) late, after autophagosome formation at 20 weeks of age (Fig. 3a–d).

Plasma ACBP levels were indistinguishable in 6-week-old Alms1-/- and WT mice, but significantly increased in obese 20-week-old Alms1-/- mice (Fig. 3h). Following 24 hours (h) of caloric restriction (starvation), 6-week-old Alms1-/- mice demonstrated the capacity to release intracellular ACBP, in the same manner as occurs in WT mice (Fig. 3i). Moreover, both Alms1-/- and WT mice exhibited similar weight loss upon starvation (Supplementary Fig. 3d). Hence, despite underlying deficiencies in basal autophagy, Alms1-/- mice respond to autophagic stimuli.

There is no evidence that the anti-ACBP mAb would reach the intracellular space, but prior studies indicate that extracellular ACBP elicits a feedforward loop elevating the expression of intracellular ACBP due to a cascade of events that involves activation of GABA A receptor 1 (to which ACBP binds via an interaction with the γ2 chain) and the PPARγ-mediated transactivation of the DBI gene, which encodes for ACBP32,35. For this reason, inhibition of extracellular ACBP diminishes intracellular ACBP levels32,35. To elucidate the effects of ALMS1 on autophagy and intracellular ACBP levels, we isolated primary hepatocytes from both WT and Alms1-/- mice. Alms1-/- hepatocytes contained higher levels of FASN, p62/SQSTM1 and ACBP (Fig. 3j, k). Similarly, depletion of ALMS1 from HepG2 cells by temporary knockdown (KD) of Alms1 with siRNAs (Fig. 3l, m and Supplementary Fig. 3e) or stable knockout (KO) of Alms1 by CRISPR-Cas9 technology (Fig. 3n–p and Supplementary Fig. 3f, g) increased the intracellular abundance of ACBP by approximately 50% compared to control cells.

ACBP neutralization and lipid metabolism in ALMS1 models
Previous research has established an obesogenic role for ACBP, which stimulates lipogenesis. Therefore, we investigated whether ACBP contributes to the phenotypic manifestations of ALMS1-deficient mice. For this, we reduced the elevated levels of ACBP observed in Alms1-/- mice by administration of an anti-ACBP monoclonal antibody (mAb) or, as a control, an isotype-matched (IgG2) irrelevant antibody for 4 weeks. In WT mice, neutralization of ACBP with this mAb and the conditional knockout of ACBP is known to have similar metabolic consequences, including a reduction in food intake, a switch from lipo-anabolism to lipo-catabolism, anti-obesity and antidiabetic effects, and protection of various organs against cytotoxic insults35,36. These findings suggest that anti-ACBP mAb mediated its effects through on-target mechanisms. The treatment of Alms1-/- mice with mAb involved two approaches: (i) curative, consisting in the treatment of 20-week-old mice with an established AöS phenotype for 4 weeks (Supplementary Fig. 4a); or (ii) preventive, consisting in the treatment of 6-week-old mice without an AöS phenotype for 4 weeks (Supplementary Fig. 4b). In the curative approach, anti-ACBP mAb failed to cause weight reduction in Alms1-/- mice compared to the IgG2 isotype-treated control mAb (Fig. 4a), although anti-ACBP mAb reduced food intake (Supplementary Fig. 4c). However, in the prophylactic approach, anti-ACBP mAb achieved significant prevention of weight gain in Alms1-/- mice (Fig. 4b) but not in WT mice compared to isotype controls (Supplementary Fig. 4d). This preventive effect on weight gain was confirmed in experiments in which anti-ACBP mAb was administered to 4-week-old Alms1-/- mice (Supplementary Fig. 4e). Of note, in the preventive setting, ACBP neutralization also normalized the glucose tolerance test in Alms1-/- mice (Fig. 4c). In parallel, injection of anti-ACBP mAb into Alms1-/- mice caused a decrease in organ weight, adipocyte size, liver and brown adipose tissue lipid content (Fig. 4d, e and Supplementary Fig. 4f–j), as well as liver FASN protein levels (Fig. 4f, g) but failed to affect liver p62/SQSTM1 levels (Fig. 4f, g). We also isolated primary hepatocytes from WT and Alms1-/- mice and treated them with the same anti-ACBP mAb (Fig. 4h, i) or silenced Acbp with siRNAs (Supplementary Fig. 4l, m). Both methods of ACBP inhibition decreased FASN levels but failed to reduce SQSTM1 abundance.

Finally, we probed lipogenic labeling in Alms1⁻/⁻ mice by intraperitoneal administration of ¹³C-labeled glucose (Supplementary Fig. 4n). Under these conditions, we observed a significant uncoupling of ¹³C-glycerol-3-phosphate (gly3P), increased in plasma and decreased in liver, compatible with rapid utilization toward esterification (Supplementary Fig. 4o). In contrast, hepatic ¹³C-palmitate enrichment 2h after ¹³C-glucose injection was directionally higher in obese Alms1-/- than in WT mice (unpaired two-sided Student’s t test; two-sided nominal P-value = 0.049; exact values are shown in Source Data) and positively correlated with body weight, but this difference did not remain significant after correction for multiple comparisons (Fig. 4j, k). Collectively these tracer data are consistent with lipid-anabolic signatures, but do not establish causal changes in de novo lipogenesis rates, which would require dedicated flux analyses.

Multi-omics after ACBP neutralization in Alms1-/- mice
To further investigate the metabolic impact of ACBP neutralization on Alms1-/- mice in the preventive setting, we conducted integrated multi-omics analyses, including metabolomics, transcriptomics, and proteomics, focused on the liver, the primary target tissue (Fig. 5, Supplementary Fig. 5 and Supplementary Data 3, 7–8).

Across all omics methods, we observed that ACBP neutralization reversed significant changes at the early disease stage (10 weeks of age), indicated by opposing log fold changes (FC) in untreated WT vs Alms1-/- tissues and anti-ACBP mAb-treated vs untreated Alms1-/- tissues (Supplementary Fig. 5). The metabolomic, transcriptomic and proteomic (Fig. 5a–c) alterations observed in Alms1-/- mice negatively correlated with the modulations observed after the treatment with anti-ACBP mAb (Pearson correlation value for the combined dataset: r = −0.82) showing a close-to-complete normalization of the Alms1-/- phenotype by ACBP neutralization (Fig. 5d).

Previously, Fig. 2 demonstrated the multiple metabolic changes in obese mice, whether induced by HFD and/or by the Alms1 mutation. Among these alterations, we observed that the anti-ACBP treatment is able to reverse changes common to both types of obesity (Fig. 5e and Supplementary Fig. 2b), such as alterations in folic acid, acylated phosphatidylcholine (15:0) or dihydrobiopterin. However, there are other metabolic changes reversed by the treatment that are exclusively Alms1-/- dependent (not observed in the HFD model) (Figs. 5e and 2c and Supplementary Data 3). These include the reversal of increased succinic acid and gluconic acid, as well as the decrease in malic acid, 3-methylhistidine, and acylated phosphatidylcholines (17:0), indicating a correction of metabolic and mitochondrial dysfunction that is Alms1 mutation-dependent rather than a mere consequence of reduced weight.

At the level of the hepatic transcriptome (Fig. 5f) Alms1-/- mice manifested altered transcription of key genes involved in energy, lipid, and mitochondrial metabolism. ACBP neutralization reduced transcription of lipogenic genes such as Cd36, Cidec, Fasn, Srebf1, and Scd1, which are associated with lipid accumulation. Conversely, ACBP neutralization increased transcription of genes related to lipolysis, such as Angptl4, Cyp4f13, Cyp4f15, Cyp7b1, Pla2g7, and Ppp2r1a, as well as that of other genes like Irs2, Pck1, and Slc7a2, suggesting an improvement in glucose homeostasis and insulin sensitivity (Supplementary Data 7).

In terms of the hepatic proteome, ACBP neutralization induced relatively few changes in enzymes involved in lipid metabolism in Alms1-/- mice (Fig. 5g). Nonetheless, the decrease in Hadhb (hydroxyacyl-CoA dehydrogenase trifunctional multienzyme complex beta subunit) is noteworthy, suggesting reduced use of beta-oxidation in a fat-burning context (Supplementary Data 8).

Overall, these data suggest that ACBP neutralization normalizes shifts in lipid, energy, and glucose metabolism in the liver from Alms1-/- mice, in accord with the normalization of other parameters such as weight gain.

ACBP neutralization and gut microbiota in Alms1-/- mice
The fecal microbiota of WT or Alms1-/- mice that were treated with isotype control or anti-ACBP mAb showed no significant differences in diversity or richness (Supplementary Fig. 6a, b). However, significant differences were found in composition (Supplementary Fig. 6c) at the phylum and genus levels (Supplementary Fig. 6d and Supplementary Data 9). To explore genotype- vs obesity-dependent effects, we included three controls: 3-week-old WT and Alms1-/- mice (which are still lean) and 10-week-old mice with high-fat diet (HFD)-induced obesity (Fig. 6a–d and Supplementary Fig. 6d). This initial analysis allowed us to evaluate the modulated taxa in the 10-week-old obese Alms1-/- mice and analyzed their potential causes, as well as the ability of the mAb treatment to reverse these changes. Alms1-/- obese mice, exhibited a decrease in Akkermansia, Alistipes, Allobaculum, Prevotella, Ruminococcaceae, and an increase in Anaeroplasma, Clostridiales, Desulfovibrio, Desulfovibrionaceae, Lactobacillus, Rikenellaceae_AF12, Rikenellaceae and Roseburia (Fig. 6c, e). Notably, only the increase in Desulfovibrio was already observed in lean 3-week-old Alms1-/- mice (Fig. 6c). Many Alms1-/- mutation associated changes (e.g., in Allobaculum, Akkermansia, Roseburia, and Clostridiales) also appeared in DIO, whereas others, such as increased Desulfovibrio and Rikenellaceae_AF12 and decreased Ruminococcaceae and Alistipes, were specifically associated with the Alms1-/- genotype (Fig. 6d).

Using the global FDR-controlled differential-abundance analysis, anti-ACBP treatment in Alms1-/- mice was associated with significant changes in a small set of taxa, decreases in Adlercreutzia, Butyricicoccus, Candidatus Arthromitus and Desulfovibrio, and increases in Lachnospiraceae and Ruminococcus (q<0.05; Supplementary Data 9). To prioritize targeted post-hoc testing, we first selected candidate taxa from the baseline WT vs Alms1-/- contrast using LEfSe (Fig. 6e), and then evaluated the treatment contrast (WT vs Alms1-/- vs treated Alms1-/- mice) with Tukey-adjusted post-hoc tests in those taxa. This specific analysis revealed that there were no effects of treatment in some taxa, even reversing the obesogenic phenotype (Supplementary Fig. 6e). However, we observed reversions of the Alms1-linked dysbiosis after anti-ACBP, with Desulfovibrio, Roseburia, Rikenellaceae_AF12, and Ruminococcaceae moving toward Alms1 WT levels (Fig. 6f). Importantly, Desulfovibrio satisfied both criteria, remaining significant under the FDR analysis and in the Tukey contrasts, and was already elevated at the presymptomatic stage, highlighting it as a priority taxon for follow-up.

## Methods

Inclusion & ethics statement
This study complies with all relevant ethical regulations. All procedures involving animals were conducted in accordance with the European Directive 2010/63/EU, Spanish Royal Decree 53/2013, and the NIH Guide for the Care and Use of Laboratory Animals. Experimental protocols were reviewed and approved by the Animal Welfare Body of the Universidad Complutense de Madrid and by the Animal Experimentation Ethics Committee of the Comunidad de Madrid (protocol PROEX012_8-21).

Animals and treatments
The “Fat Aussie” (NOD.B10-Alms1^foz/foz) mouse strain was kindly provided by Dr. Christopher C. Goodnow53 and maintained in the animal facility at Complutense University of Madrid under specific pathogen-free conditions with 12h light/12h dark cycle and temperature (19–23°C) and relative humidity (45–65%) according to FELASA guidelines. Only male mice were used in this study to avoid the potential confounding effects of the estrous cycle on metabolic, transcriptomic, proteomic, and microbiota profiles. Since hormonal fluctuations in females can introduce additional variability, male mice were selected to improve the reproducibility and consistency of the data across the multi-omics analyses performed.

After genotyping, healthy male mice were used. For experiments without microbiota, animals were stratified by litter and basal body weight and randomly assigned (computer-generated list) to the corresponding diet and, where applicable, treatment. Experimental cages contained randomly selected male mice to mitigate potential effects of cage-specific microbial changes. Importantly, the observed phenotypic differences between groups remained robust regardless of the cohousing strategy, supporting the reliability of our conclusions. For microbiota experiments, the cohousing strategy was designed to prevent microbiota exchange through coprophagy. Samples were collected from cages containing mice under identical experimental conditions to ensure consistency. To control covariates in metabolomics, we applied the predefined inclusion window (±10% body-weight and glycemia).

Male mice received normal chow (LASQCdiet, cat. D.Rod18.H; protein 18.9%, fat 5.3%, fiber 3.9 %, ash 7.0 %; with vitamins and minerals) with access to water ad libitum. To obtain the DIO-mice model, male animals were fed with a high fat diet (HFD) (Envigo cat. MD.2204 Adjusted 60/Fat Diet, protein 23%, fat 34%, fiber 5%, ash 5%; with vitamins and minerals) with an excess of dietary fats until 10 weeks old. Diets were supplied as pellets (16 mm) and stored at 4°C.

On breeding, the genotype was verified by polymerase chain reaction (PCR) using genomic DNA isolated from tail biopsies with specific primer pairs detailed in Supplementary Data 10. PCR products were separated by electrophoresis in 4% agarose gels (R0492, Thermo Fisher Scientific) and visualized using GelRed (BT-41003, Biogen).

Tissues were snap-frozen in liquid nitrogen, extracted and homogenized in 20mM Tris buffer (pH 7.4) containing 150mM NaCl, 1% Triton X-100, 10mM EDTA, phosphatase inhibitor cocktail (4906837001, Roche) and protease inhibitor cocktail tablets (11836170001, Roche). Tissue extracts were then centrifuged at 10000 xg (4°C), and supernatants were collected. Protein concentration in supernatants was evaluated by the bicinchoninic acid technique (23225, Pierce Biotechnology). Plasma was harvested from blood collection tubes by centrifugation at 10000 xg for 30min.

Male mice were analyzed at baseline or after one month of treatment with a monoclonal antibody against ACBP or isotype IgG (Bioxcell, NH, USA) (2.5µg/g body weight, BW intraperitoneally in 200µL of saline) administered in 5 doses, once per week. Leupeptin (30mg/kg BW; 108976, Sigma-Aldrich) was used in vivo by intraperitoneal injection 6h before the end of the experiment.

Presymptomatic cohorts consisted of 6-week-old male mice, and symptomatic cohorts were 20-week-old. Prevention studies used mice at 6 weeks of age, administered the assigned treatment for 4 weeks, and were analyzed at 10 weeks, and curative studies started treatment at 20 weeks of age and were analyzed at 24 weeks.

ACBP detection in murine plasma samples
ACBP levels in plasma were determined using a specific ELISA kit (MBS2025156, MyBioSource) as instructed by the manufacturer.

Glucose tolerance test (GTT)
Male animals were fasted for 16h and given an intraperitoneal injection of glucose (2.5g/kg BW). Blood was collected each 30min from the lateral vein of the tail prior to and at the indicated time points after the injection. Glucose was measured using a precision glucometer (Accu-Chek Performa).

¹³C-Glucose tracing
To assess lipid metabolism, mice completed a 4-week preventive anti-ACBP treatment; the last antibody dose was given 30min before tracer administration. After an overnight fast, mice received an intraperitoneal injection of anti-ACBP monoclonal antibody or isotype IgG control. Thirty minutes later, mice were injected i.p. with [U-¹³C₆]-D-glucose (Merck/Sigma-Aldrich, 389374; 2.5gkg⁻¹ in saline). Two hours after tracer injection, mice were euthanized, and plasma and liver were collected. ¹³C-labeled metabolites were quantified by mass spectrometry.

Food intake analysis
Male mice were housed and acclimated to the chambers for 48h before experimental measurements and food intake was measured by weighting the food consumed by mice each 6h.

Histology
After fixation of liver and white adipose tissues, 4µm thick paraffin sections were stained with hematoxylin and eosin. Each slide was examined using a Zeiss Axiophot microscope.

Cell culture and treatments
HepG2 cells (HB-806, ATCC) obtained from human hepatocellular carcinoma were cultured at 37°C under 5% CO2 in Dulbecco’s Modified Eagle Medium (DMEM) (41966029, Gibco) containing D-glucose 25mM, sodium pyruvate 1mM, L-glutamine 4mM, and supplemented with 10% heat-inactivated fetal bovine (10500064, Gibco), HEPES buffer 1M (15630056, Gibco), and 10000 units/mL penicillin G sodium and 100000µg/mL streptomycin sulfate (15140122, Gibco). Cells were seeded in 6–12-well plates and grown for 36h before treatment with 50nM BafA1 (S-S1413, Selleckchem), EBSS medium (24010043, Gibco) or anti-ACBP (or respective isotype control) in vitro (1–10µg/mL; ab232760, Abcam). Treatments were maintained for a period of 4h.

Primary hepatocyte isolation and cultures
Mice were injected intraperitoneally with 150µL of 1000U/mL heparin 5min prior to anesthesia with a ketamine/xylazine mixture (30mg/mL and 6mg/mL, respectively, in saline serum) 3.75µL/g body weight. Once the mouse was properly anesthetized and didn’t present signs of consciousness nor reflexes, the abdomen was vertically cut to have access to the vena cava. Perfusion was initiated by attaching a catheter to the inferior vena cava, followed by a sequence of perfusion solutions (1.50mL EBSS w/o Ca&Mg + 250µL 100mM EGTA, 2.30mL EBSS with Ca&Mg + 10mM HEPES (pH 7.4), and 3.2×50mL Solution 2 + 0.3mg/mL Collagenase + 0.04mg/mL trypsin inhibitor 100cdu/mL − 100mL) pre-heated at 42°C. Liver digestion was monitored, and after sufficient digestion, the liver was transferred to Solution 4 (Williams E medium + 2mM (1%) L-glutamine + 1% Penicillin/Streptomycin + 10% FBS) and disrupted with a forceps for posterior cell isolation. Hepatocytes were filtered through a 100µm cell strainer, centrifuged a 500×g for 3min 4°C, and washed with Williams E medium 3 times. Living hepatocytes were then counted using Trypan blue and plated on 6-well plates (106 cells per well). After 4–6h, plated hepatocytes were washed with sterile PBS, and the media (Solution 4) was renewed before subsequent assays54,55. Materials: water (50mL), ethanol (50mL), peristaltic pump, water bath, Falcon tube holders (9-tube and 16-tube), Vacutainer Safety-Lok Blood Collection Set, syringes (1mL), 27G needles, paper roll, tray, tape, and various reagents including calcium and magnesium-free EBSS (Gibco™, 12539069), EGTA, HEPES, Williams E medium (Gibco™, 11570606), L-glutamine, penicillin/streptomycin, fetal bovine serum (FBS), collagenase type IV (Thermo, 17104019), trypsin inhibitor (Merck, T6522), heparin, ketamine, and xylazine. Solutions were prepared for hepatocyte isolation, including EGTA-EBSS, HEPES-EBSS, and a collagenase solution. Equipment was set up prior to the experiment, including a water bath (42°C), a peristaltic pump, and a cell culture hood, with sterile pipettes, Petri dishes, and other consumables prepared.

RNA interference and plasmid transfection
Full details of all oligonucleotides and plasmids are found in Supplementary Data 10. Cells were transfected at 50–60% confluence using medium without antibiotics. Specific siRNAs for ACBP and/or ALMS1 were reverse transfected at a concentration of 10nM using Lipofectamine RNAi MaxTM Transfection Reagent (13778075, Invitrogen) for 36–48h before treatments. A scrambled siRNA was always used as a control, and siRNA-mediated protein downregulation was controlled by immunoblotting. The CRISPR/Cas9 ALMS1-encoding plasmids (KN414632, OriGene) were also applied by lipofectamine transfection according to the manufacturer’s instructions, and cells were analyzed after puromycin (P8833, Sigma) selection. The insertion of the linear donor was verified by PCR (Supplementary Data 10). To confirm transfection, cells were fixed in 4% paraformaldehyde for 15min at room temperature, and GFP fluorescence was assessed (Leica DMI 3000 microscope; Leica AG, Wetzlar, Germany).

ACBP detection in culture medium
ACBP levels in culture medium were determined using a specific human ELISA kit (KA0532-96, Abnova) as instructed by the manufacturer.

Immunoblotting
For immunoblotting, tissue or cellular proteins were collected and resuspended in 50mM Tris buffer (pH 7.4) containing 250mM NaCl, 0.5% NP-40, 5mM EDTA, 50mM NaF, phosphatase inhibitor cocktail (4906837001, Roche Applied Science) and protease inhibitor cocktail tablets (11836170001, Roche Applied Science) and 15–20µg were loaded on 4–12% polyacrylamide gel (5678094, Biorad). The gels were initially run without the protein samples for 60min at 70V, followed by the inclusion of samples for a duration of 60–90min at 110–130V, aimed at enhancing the separation of smaller proteins. Samples are electrotransferred to PVDF membranes (3010040001, Roche), which were horizontally sliced according to the molecular weight of the protein of interest to allow simultaneous detection within the same experiment. Unspecific binding sites were saturated by incubating membranes for 1hour in 0.1% Tween-20 (BP337-100, Fisher Bioreagents) (v:v in TBS) supplemented with 5% non-fat powdered milk (w:v in TBS), followed by overnight incubation with specifics primary and secondary antibodies: ACBP (human, Abcam ab16871, rabbit pAb, 1:1000, lot GR121034-6); ACBP (mouse, Abcam ab231910, rabbit pAb, 1:1000, lots GR3413135-1; GR3236201-4); ALMS1 (Abcam ab84892, rabbit pAb, 1:1000, lot GR288319-18); FASN (Abcam Ab22759, rabbit pAb, 1:1000, lot Gr3422783-1); GAPDH (CST#2118, clone 14C10, rabbit mAb, 1:5000, lots 14; 16); LC3B (CST#2775, rabbit pAb, 1:1000, lots 14; 13); p62/SQSTM1 (Abnova #H00008878 M01, clone 2C11, mouse IgG2a, 1:5000, lots M591-2C11; N3131-2C11). Secondary antibodies: anti-rabbit IgG–HRP (Sigma A0545, goat pAb, 1:5000, lot 0000130704) and anti-mouse IgG–HRP (Sigma A9044, rabbit pAb, 1:5000, lots 0000118493; 0000127278). All info is also detailed in Supplementary Data 10. Signals from the protein bands were detected using chemiluminescence (EPN2235, Cytiva Amersham).

Gene expression analysis
Total RNA from cell lines was purified using QIAwave RNA Mini Kit (74536, QIAGEN) and total RNA from murine tissues was isolated by trituration with a motorized micro pestle, followed by column purification with QIAwave RNA Mini Kit (74536, QIAGEN). Following the manufacturer’s instructions, the High-Capacity cDNA Reverse Transcription Kit (10400745, Applied Biosystems) was used for the generation of cDNA. Quantitative PCR was performed on a StepOnePlus Real-Time PCR System (Applied Biosystems) using PowerUp SYBR Green (A25777, Applied Biosystems). All oligonucleotide sequences are provided in Supplementary Data 10 together with catalog numbers, annealing temperatures and amplicon sizes.

Metabolome analysis
Samples were treated following the protocol described previously56 to extract metabolites. Briefly, 50µL of serum were vortexed with 500µL of ice-cold extraction mixture (MeOH/water, 9/1, −20°C, with a cocktail of internal standards) for 5min, and then centrifuged (10min at 15000 xg, 4°C). Regarding the tissue, 30mg were weighed and homogenized by a Precellys (Bertin) protocol (3 cycles, 5500rpm), then centrifuged (10min at 15000 xg, 4°C). After, several fractions of the supernatant were split to be analyzed by different Liquid and Gas chromatographies coupled with mass spectrometers (LC/MS and GC/MS) as previously described57.

Widely targeted analyses were performed by GC and LC MS couplings. GC-MS/MS was performed on a 7890A gas chromatography (Agilent Technologies) coupled to a QQQ (triple quadrupole) 7000C (Agilent Technologies). Bile acids, polyamines and short chain-fatty acids analyses were performed by LC-MS/MS with a 1290 UHPLC (Ultra-High Performance Liquid Chromatography) (Agilent Technologies) coupled to a QQQ 6470 (Agilent Technologies). Widely pseudo-targeted analysis by UHPLC-HRMS (Ultra-High Performance Liquid Chromatography – High Resolution Mass Spectrometer) was performed on a Dionex U3000/Orbitrap q-Exactive (Thermo) coupling.

All targeted treated data were merged then cleaned by mean of a dedicated R package (@Github/Kroemerlab/GRMeta). Complete codes are available in the repository https://github.com/kroemerlab. R was used to perform bioinformatic analyses. Differentially expressed metabolites were identified using linear models (Limma), and P-values adjusted for multiple comparisons by applying the Benjamini-Hochberg correction. Differences were considered significant when P < 0.05 and FDR Q < 0.25. Heatmaps and volcano plots were generated using the heatmap3 and EnhancedVolcano packages, respectively. Glimma was used for interactive visualizations. Functional metabolite annotation was performed using Metaboanalyst.

13C labeling and analysis
Sample preparation for labeling analysis: Murine tissues (around 30mg) were weighted and transferred to 2mL-homogenizer tubes with ceramic beads (Precellys, Bertin Technologies), containing 1mL of ice-cold extraction mixture (metOH/water, 9/1, −20°C). The samples were homogenized in Precellys 24 tissue homogenizer (3 cycles of 20s/5000rpm), followed by centrifugation (15min at 10000 xg, 4°C). Murine plasma (25µL) was mixed at 2500rpm during 5min with 500µL of ice-cold extraction mixture (metOH/water, 9/1, −20°C) and centrifuged (15min at 10000 xg, 4°C). Supernatants were split as previously described56.

Labeling experiment by targeted analysis of glycolysis pathway by ion pairing ultra-high performance liquid chromatography (UHPLC) coupled to a Triple Quadrupole (QQQ) mass spectrometer
Targeted analysis is performed on an RRLC 1290 system (Agilent Technologies) coupled to a Triple Quadrupole 6470 (Agilent Technologies) equipped with an electrospray source operating in negative mode. Palmitic acid was measured in liver samples by liquid chromatography coupled to mass spectrometry (LC-MS). To accurately assess de novo lipogenesis from exogenous ¹³C-glucose, we focused our analysis on the heavier isotopologues of palmitic acid (M+4, m/z 259). This isotopologue more reliably reflects glucose-derived fatty acid synthesis, as their presence is not significantly influenced by the natural isotopic abundance of palmitate or by pre-existing unlabeled lipid pools. In contrast, M+2 (m/z 257) may include a substantial endogenous contribution due to the natural presence of ¹³C and ¹8O, which could confound interpretation. Therefore, M+4 was selected as the most specific indicator of newly synthesized palmitate.

In-solution trypsin digestion: 200µL of solution were mixed with 100µL of 25mM ammonium bicarbonate buffer pH 8.5, reduced by adding 30µL of 10mM DTT and incubated at 56°C for 20min. The nebulizer gas pressure was set to 35psi, whereas the drying gas flow was set to 10 L/min at a temperature of 250°C, and the sheath gas flow was set to 12 L/min at a temperature of 300°C. MS and MS/MS mass range was 50–1700 m/z and scan rates were 8 spectra/sec for MS and 3 spectra/sec for MS/MS. Auto MS/MS mode was used with precursor selection by abundance and a maximum of 20 precursors selected per cycle. A ramped collision energy was used with a slope of 3.6 and an offset of −4.8. The same ion was rejected after two consecutive scans. Data processing and analysis was performed Spectrum Mill MS Proteomics Workbench (Rev B.04.01, Agilent Technologies, Santa Clara, CA, USA). Briefly, raw data were extracted under default conditions as follows: non fixed or variable modifications were selected; [MH]+ 50–10000 m/z; maximum precursor charge +5; retention time and m/z tolerance ±60s; minimum signal-to-noise MS (S/N) 25; finding 12C signals. Validation of peptide and protein data was performed using the auto-validational algorithm for validation of peptide and protein data. The exact FASTA file (UniProtKB/Swiss-Prot Mus musculus reference proteome (17,170 reviewed entries; file UniProt.mouse.fasta; MD5=6015ca1e9465cb64a8be4451dc581ef8) supplemented with a database of common contaminants (cRAP) and its manifest are deposited with the dataset (MassIVE MSV000099335).

Enrichment study of biological pathways. Over Representation Analysis (ORA) using the Gene Ontology (Biological Processes)58,59 or the Kyoto Encyclopedia of Genes and Genomes (KEGG) databases60–62. We accounted for multiple testing using the Benjamini-Hochberg method, with FDR < 0.05. All analyses were performed using R Statistical Software (v4.4.1; R Core Team 2021) with the Bioconductor package “clusterProfiler”63.

Transcriptomic analysis
mRNA-seq. Total RNA is treated with beads poliT, which binds with poliA tail present in eukaryotic mRNAs. After this, it is recovered only mRNAs with beads poliT and beads poliT are removed in order to get only mRNAs. The library step is done using these mRNAs with the typical steps of a library construction using commercial kit called Truseq stranded mRNA Library from Illumina. Sequencing step was done with a 150 PE read length and with a minimum of 40M reads/sample in an Illumina sequencer NovaSeq6000 Bioinformatics: The bioinformatics analysis was performed by Dreamgenics S.L. First, raw FASTQ files were evaluated using FastQC [https://www.bioinformatics.babraham.ac.uk/projects/fastqc/] quality checks, and sequence trimming was performed to remove bases, adapters, and other low-quality sequences with fastp [https://github.com/OpenGene/fastp] software. Next, pseudo-alignment of the sequences against the reference transcriptome for Mus musculus GRCm39 (Gencode: release M32) [https://www.gencodegenes.org/mouse/release_M32.html] and direct quantification of transcripts were carried out using Salmon (v1.10.0) [https://combine-lab.github.io/salmon/]. For differential expression analysis between conditions, the DESeq2 [https://bioconductor.org/packages/release/bioc/html/DESeq2.html] algorithm was used; said analysis was carried out considering the adjusted p-value, using the Benjamini-Hochberg method for adjusting the P-value (padj). Genes with an adjusted P-value less than 0.05 and a log2 Fold Change greater than 1 or less than −1 were considered differentially expressed.

Analyses of the mice gut microbiota
The total DNA per sample was extracted from 200mg of feces using the QIAamp Power Fecal Pro DNA Kit (Qiagen). Illumina libraries of the V3-V4 region of the 16S rRNA gene were prepared following the manufacturer’s instructions. High-throughput sequencing was performed with a MiSeq Illumina sequencer (2×300bp) by the Translational Genomics (NGS) Unit of the Ramón y Cajal Hospital https://www.irycis.org/en/services/11/translational-genomics-ngs. The Quantitative Insights into Microbial Ecology (QIIME2) pipeline (version qiime2-2020.8) was used to perform the quality filtering, discard chimeric sequences, merge the paired-end reads and estimate the Amplicon Single Variants (ASVs)64. The ASV calculation was based on the DADA2 method implemented in QIIME2 https://qiime2.org/. The Greengenes database65,66 was used for the taxonomic assignment, and the analyses were performed at the genus level. Read clusters that not reaching the genus level were assigned to the last well-identified taxonomic assignation. The alpha-diversity metrics Shannon Index (diversity) and Chao1 (richness) were calculated with the “microbiome” R package “https://github.com/microbiome/microbiome”. To statistically compare the metric distribution between groups, we used the Wilcoxon signed-rank test with Benjamini-Hochberg correction to adjust for multiple comparisons implemented in the R core. The composition patterns between samples were explored with the non-metric multidimensional scaling (NMDS) based on Bray-Curtis dissimilarity. We estimated the significance of the differences between groups with the Permutational multivariate analysis of variance (PERMANOVA) in the R package Vegan: https://github.com/vegandevs/vegan. To identify the taxa associated with the experimental groups, we used the LefSe method (R package microbial) https://github.com/guokai8/microbial67.

Statistical & reproducibility
Data are reported as the mean±SEM, as specified. The number of independent data points (n, individual mice values or number of independent experiments), P-values and statistical tests used are indicated in the figures and legends of the corresponding figures. Two-group comparisons used unpaired, two-sided Student’s t tests (or Wilcoxon tests for non-normal microbiota diversity metrics). Multi-group designs used one-way ANOVA with Tukey correction; mixed designs (age × genotype) used two-way mixed-effects models with Sidak correction. Correlations used two-sided Pearson’s r. Omics-wide analyses (metabolome, transcriptome, proteome) and microbiota differential taxa used multiple-testing control (Benjamini–Hochberg FDR; LEfSe where indicated). Beta-diversity differences were tested by PERMANOVA. Statistical significance was defined as P < 0.05 and exact P-values, test names, tailing (two-sided), effect sizes and n are reported in figures and legends. We did not perform formal a priori power calculations. Group sizes were guided by pilot data and literature while balancing statistical power with the 3Rs. Primary in vivo endpoints targeted effects of ~20–30% (SD ~10–15%), for which n ≈ 8 per group gives ~80% power at α = 0.05. Sample sizes by modality were: histology and immunoblotting (n=5–6/group; large effects, blinded scoring, tissue-processing throughput); metabolomics (n=8/group; a predefined inclusion window restricted analysis to 8 mice per group whose body weight and blood glucose were within the target range to isolate the effects of obesity genotype); transcriptomics (n=7–8/group; instrument time/cost); proteomics (n=5/group; instrument time/cost); microbiota (n=5–6/group; cage considered the experimental unit when appropriate); 13C-lipid screening (n=4–5/group; one mouse died before sacrifice for unknown reasons and was not analyzed); leupeptin-flow controls (n=3/group; mechanistic confirmation, limited cohort); primary hepatocytes (n=3 independent isolations). In vitro assays were repeated across n=3 independent experiments; ≥50 images/condition were quantified with fixed, pre-set parameters.

Researchers were not blinded during animal handling or sample collection, as genotype and diet produced obvious phenotypes, and microbiota analyses required group-specific housing and labeling. To limit bias, endpoints and analyses settings were predefined and based on objective instrument readings. Mouse tissue analyses were performed blindly and were analyzed after the corresponding parameters (hepatic steatosis and adipocyte size) had been determined. The Omics datasets were also processed using coded sample IDs, and the group labels were revealed at the time of analysis.

No post-hoc data exclusions were made, apart from: (i) applying the a priori predefined inclusion window for metabolomics (±10% around cohort mean body weight and glycemia) to isolate genotype effects from obesity; and (ii) one animal that died immediately before sampling, which was therefore not analyzed.

## Round 1 — Reviewer Comments

### Reviewer 1

The present study aims at linking extracellular levels of ACBP to the development of ciliopathic obesity. The authors use mice carrying a mutation in the ALMS1 gene, a model of Alström syndrome, which clinically manifests in metabolic problems, including insulin resistance, diabetes, obesity, and liver abnormalities, and non-metabolic symptoms including sensorineural hearing loss, retinal degeneration and cardiomyopathy. They take a systems-wide biology approach using LC/MS based metabolomics, proteomics and sequencing to identify putative links between metabolism, autophagy and microbiome and argues that inactivation of ACBP in the circulation can prevent the metabolic manifestations of Alms1-/- mice. Unfortunately, the study relies on using neutralizing antibodies against ACBP and not genetically ablated ACBP mice. The study is interesting, however there are major issues that prevent the manuscript from being acceptable for publication in Nature Communication.
Major issues:
1. The authors initially use metabolomics to show that functional loss of ALMS1 affects the metabolome in liver, adipose and plasma. Yet this is an interesting phenotype of Alms1-/- mice, this part of the study seems to be disconnected from the parts revolving around ACBP. The authors later argue that neutralizing ACBP using antibodies can prevent the development of the metabolic manifestations of AöS in Alms1-/- mice. Thus, the authors need to show how neutralizing ACBP in Alms1-/- mice can restore these metabolic manifestations using metabolomics. To this end, the authors need to genetically target ACBP in Alms1-/- mice to show that this also restore the metabolic manifestations.
2. An overall shortage of the entire study is the lack of using ACBP knock out mice. The authors solely rely on using neutralizing antibodies in an effort to link ACBP levels to the metabolic manifestations of Alms1 mice. The authors must experimentally use ACBP knock out animals to strengthen the point of the study.
3. All WBs show ACBP as a 14 kDA, yet ACBP is normally considered as a 10 kDa protein of 86 amino acids. The authors must clearly indicate which isoform of ACBP they are targeting by siRNA, antibodies etc. To this end, as the authors use siRNA to knock down ACBP in cell lines (HepG2), how does siRNA affect expression levels of other ACBP isoforms?
4. Figure 4; the authors argue that there is an effect on lipogenesis, yet they only provide expression levels of selected genes involved in lipogenesis. They must experimentally show that there is an effect on de novo fatty acid- and lipid synthesis using e.g. tracer analyses.
5. Figure 7 summarizes the findings and along with the text, the authors indicate that ACBP neutralizing antibodies also will target intracellular ACBP. What is the evidence for antibodies reaching intracellular ACBP.? Again, if the neutralizing antibodies have an effect on ACBP and thus on lipogenesis and metabolic manifestations, the authors must use ACBP KO animals to confirm their findings. Can the observed phenotypes be ascribed to targeting of intracellular ACBP and not extracellular ACBP per se?
6. For all WBs, it is unclear how many independent samples that are loaded? Is a sample in one lane a pool of several samples from replicate experiments? or does N equal one? At least three independent replicates for one treatment must be shown.
7. There is no info on which antibodies that have been used. The authors must provide specific catalog numbers/info to inform which specific protein the antibodies have been raised against.
8. The authors solely discuss ACBP as an extracellular protein. Yet, it was first identified as an intracellular protein involved in termination of fatty acid synthesis. The authors must elaborate the role of ACBP in lipid metabolism throughout the manuscript, both its intracellular role as well as its extracellular role.
Minor:
1. Suppl. table 5 is missing

### Reviewer 2

This is an interesting study that seeks to understand the underlying mechanism by which AoS results in weight gain and metabolic syndrome. It utilizes unbiased profiling methods to look at metabolomic and transcriptomic changes, as well targeted analysis and direct perturbations of cell culture systems and mice (in this case, anti-ACBP treatment), to advance the concept that altered autophagic flux is an initiating event that affect metabolic balance through ACBP secretion. There are many interesting aspects to the story. The study however suffers in many places from lack of appropriate controls to properly deconvolute the effects of obesity per se, from genotype and/or treatment. This is a major deficiency. Secondly, the metabolic characterization of the mice is also too superficial to conclude that food intake is the only or dominant driver of obesity as implied. Lastly, there are aspects of rigor of study design and interpretation that need attention.
Specific comments are below:
1) The study needs to explicitly state the gender of the animals used in each experiment. Given the significance of gender on body weight, the data is hard to interpret without this information.
2) Animal breeding scheme and housing is also very important to the entire study and should be clearly stated. Mice should be littermates, and if microbiome as a factor is of interest, the animals should be segregated by genotype after weaning. Complete segregation of the colonies causes genetic and microbiome drifts that cannot be properly controlled and this should be avoided. If microbiome changes want to be avoided, cohousing of mutant and control animals into adulthood should be used. For this story, are the control animals littermates of the mutant mice? Where they co-housed with mutant mice or segregated at weaning, or derived from 2 parallel colonies in the same vivarium?
3) Without a diet induced obesity control group, the metabolomic disturbance in 20 wk old AoS mice is impossible to interpret (Fig 1, Fig S1). It is unclear what may be due to obesity alone and what may be the result of the AoS genetic alteration. This shortcoming is present also in many subsequent figures.
The pre-obese mice studied are less problematic, at least when they are matched by weight, but does not completely overcome the problems noted for studies of older mice as important metabolic changes seen after week 8 of life that are due to AoS may have been missed.
Whenever a key conclusion is being drawn, a diet induced obese group, weight matched to the mutant mouse, needs to be included. Alternatively, pair-feeding the mutant mice to match a control group by weight is another strategy.
4) This point of weight vs genotype vs treatment is also a problem for the interpretation of Fig 6, a key figure in the paper. AoS mutant and isotype treated mice are obese while WT isotype treated mice are lean (top comparison in panel 6A). AoS mutant and anti-ACBP treated mice are lean, where are AoS mutant and isotype treated mice are obese, exactly the reciprocal weight relationship (bottom comparison in panel 6A). The observed differences seem to correlate with weight rather than genotype or treatment. It should be noted that obesity will also drive dysbiosis, so again, results from these comparisons cannot deconvolute the contributions of weight alone, from genotype or treatment group.
5) Anti-ACPB treatment did not reverse obesity in older mice, even though it did reduce food intake considerably. The interpretation of the effect of anti-ACBP treatment is incomplete without full metabolic phenotyping of the mice. Weight matched, pre-obese mice (or pair fed mice that are weight matched), should be placed in metabolic cages to measure all the key determinants of energy balance, not just food intake, but also thermogenesis, movement, etc. Stool calorimetry should be included as well to assess caloric losses (or efficiency of caloric extraction from the diet). Beside studying mice by genotype, this experiment should be done in isotype and anti-ACBP treated mice, so that we can conclude convincingly what drives the effect of the treatment (or its failure in older mice).
6) The manuscript should avoid making any claims on non-statistically significant nominal differences. Rigorously speaking, the probability that those values are different is low, and should not be interpreted as potential differences between the groups (eg, Acc1 in Fig S5). Similarly, it is problematic to compare gene expression profiles in different groups that were not studied simultaneously (like when Fig 3B and S5H are compared). This should be avoided.

### Reviewer 3

A multi-omics study by Corral Nieto, Y. and Fernández Pereira, A.G. et al. showed that presymptomatic AöS mice had early liver dyslipidemia, impaired autophagy, and hepatic ACBP accumulation. Title: Identification of ACBP as a potential target in ciliopathic obesity through multi-
omics network analysis
First author: Yaiza Corral Nieto
Lead author: José Manuel Bravo-San Pedro
Re-submission date: 31/03/2025
General comments to the reviewers
We would like to express our sincere gratitude to the reviewers for their exceptionally thorough
and constructive evaluation during both rounds of review. Their insightful comments and
suggestions have allowed us to significantly improve the manuscript, which now includes a
complete characterization of Alström syndrome at different disease stages. Over the course of
the two rounds of review, we have integrated four comprehensive omics analyses
(metabolomics, proteomics, transcriptomics, and microbiome), providing a robust
multidimensional description of the pathophysiology and its modulation by targeting ACBP.
Moreover, we present a detailed insight into the role of cilia, autophagy, and ACBP in this
disease, and report on the preclinical efficacy of a potential therapeutic strategy. We are
convinced that these advances significantly enhance the translational value and potential impact
of our work.
Point-by-point reply to Reviewer No. 1.
Overall: The manuscript presents a compelling study linking extracellular levels of acyl-CoA
binding protein (ACBP) to ciliopathic obesity, particularly Alström syndrome (AöS), through
multi-omics approaches. The study is valuable for identifying a novel target in ACBP that could
mitigate obesity-related complications. However, the reliance on neutralizing antibodies
without using an acbp knockout model significantly weakens the mechanistic insights into the
role of ACBP, particularly when claiming its extracellular versus intracellular roles.
Our response: The reviewer raises a few additional points that we address as indicated below.
Remark No. 1 by reviewer No. 1: ACBP Neutralization with Antibodies vs. Gene Ablation:
One of the core issues is the authors' reliance on neutralizing antibodies to inhibit ACBP.
Although the authors argue that neutralizing ACBP in Alms1-/- mice prevents metabolic
manifestations, they fail to demonstrate the same through genetic ablation of acbp. As originally
was pointed out, the use of genetically modified acbp knockout mice would have provided a
more robust mechanistic understanding. In their rebuttal, the authors state that acbp ablation
leads to lethality. This is incorrect as several studies have shown that Acbp ablation in mice
results in impaired epidermal barrier resulting in among others increased systemic energy
expenditure, beiging of white adipose tissue, resistance to diet-induced obesity and improved
glucose tolerance (doi: 10.1016/j.molmet.2020.101144; doi: 10.1194/jlr.M060780; doi:
10.1016/j.celrep.2013.11.010; doi: 10.1074/jbc.M110.161109). I acknowledge that creating
such a model will take time due to the complexity of breeding required genotypes. However,
this is not an acceptable justification for excluding critical control experiments, as this leaves
open questions about how much of the observed phenotype is due to antibody targeting versus
gene ablation.
the knockout Acbp mouse model was lethal. Indeed, a non-lethal full-body ACBP knockout
mouse has already been generated (Doi: 10.1074/jbc.M110.161109). However, in 2015, we
formally requested a collaboration to the authors of this model, which was unfortunately
rejected. Furthermore, it is important to highlight that the available non-lethal ACBP knockout
model shows only a transient metabolic phenotype restricted to a narrow period between
postnatal days 20 and 30, as described by the original authors (Doi: 10.1074/jbc.M110.161109),
and the displayed Alström syndrome phenotype occurs from day 60 of life of the diseased
mouse. In fact, the authors themselves state in the Discussion section that "future investigations
using tissue-specific knock-out models are needed to establish the role of ACBP in TAG and
CE accumulation in the liver and in SREBP processing" highlighting the importance of
conditional approaches, such as the one we implemented. This situation led us to develop our
own tissue-specific ACBP conditional KO mouse to target the specific extracellular and tissue
functions of ACBP, published in Cell Metabolism in 2019.
We fully understand and appreciate the reviewer's interest in a double knockout model (DKO,
Alms1/Acbp). However, based on our experience generating the Acbp conditional knockout
model, we estimate that generating the double knockout mouse (Alms1 mutant crossed with
Acbp-floxed mice and a tissue-specific Cre line) would require approximately 18 months, due
to the complexity of breeding schemes and the need for additional approvals of animal testing
protocols according to national regulations. We believe that while this model would
undoubtedly be valuable, its generation exceeds the feasibility of the study.
Although technically more limited than a complete DKO, our current strategy provides a solid
mechanistic understanding of the extracellular role of ACBP in the context of Alström
syndrome. Moreover, it’s important to note that the effect of the neutralizing antibody used in
this study has already been compared to genetic manipulations that inhibit the Acbp system,
namely:
(i) Conditional knockout of Acbp by a ubiquitous tamoxifen-inducible CRE recombinase
excising the floxed exon 2 of the Acbp gene in adult mice (PMID: 31422903)
(ii) Point mutation of the Acbp receptor, GABRG2, in position 72, which if present in
homozygosity (genotype: Gabrg2F77I/F77I) abolishes binding of Acbp protein to the GABA
Type 1 receptor complex (PMID: 28343864, PMID: 35436993, PMID: 38582872).
For example, we showed in a model of steatohepatitis induced by a methionine/choline-
deficient diet that mAb 7G4a, knockout of Acbp and Gabrg2F77I/F77I mutation had similar
effects in inhibiting the manifestation of liver disease (PMID: 36191214). In addition, mAb
7G4a, knockout of Acbp and Gabrg2F77I/F77I mutation similarly protected the liver against high-
fat diet-induced steatosis (PMID: 35436993). Moreover, mAb 7G4a, knockout
of Acbp and Gabrg2F77I/F77I mutation have been systematically compared with respect to
their capacity to block the metabolic manifestations of Cushing syndrome induced by
supplementation with corticosterone. Thus, mAb 7G4a, knockout
of Acbp and Gabrg2F77I/F77I mutation similarly attenuated the corticosterone-induced
weight gain, hepatomegaly, visceral adiposity, sarcopenia, dyslipidemia and type-2 diabetes
(PMID: 39578649). Finally, mAb 7G4a and knockout of Acbp similarly mitigated mechanical
destabilization-induced knee osteoarthritis (PMID: 40082721).
Finally, we have added this information as a limitation in the Discussion of the revised version:
"A limitation of our study is the absence of an in vivo genetic ACBP knockout model. However,
our study incorporates in vitro models using both primary hepatocytes and HepG2 cells, in
2
which ALMS1 was genetically silenced or knocked out, supporting the relevance of our findings
at the cellular level. Nonetheless, prior studies have shown that inhibiting the ACBP system—
whether by neutralizing extracellular ACBP, knocking out the Acbp gene (thus removing both
intra- and extracellular ACBP), or mutating the ACBP receptor (thus affecting only signaling
by extracellular ACBP)—provides comparable protection against liver damage induced by
methionine-choline deficiency, hepatic steatosis triggered by high-fat diets, and high-dose
corticotherapy-induced metabolic shifts leading to visceral obesity, steatosis, dyslipidemia and
insulin resistance. These findings strongly suggest that extracellular ACBP has pathogenic
effects that can be counteracted by neutralizing antibodies acting on target. In this study, we
observed that certain metabolites, which are dysregulated exclusively in the AöS model, but
not in DIO model, are normalized by ACBP inhibition, suggesting that ACBP neutralization
may have broadly positive effects across different models of metabolic derangement.”
Remark No. 2 by reviewer No. 1: Incomplete Evidence for Lipogenesis and Lipolysis: The
authors claim an impact on lipogenesis in Alms1-/- mice treated with anti-ACBP antibodies.
However, the original reviewer's request for tracer analyses to directly quantify de novo
lipogenesis remains unaddressed. While the authors provide additional transcriptomic and
proteomic data supporting reduced lipogenesis, these are indirect measures. The authors should
have included isotope-labeled fatty acid or glucose tracers to more convincingly demonstrate
an actual decrease in lipid synthesis, strengthening their claims about the metabolic impact of
ACBP inhibition.
Our response: Thank the reviewer for this point that we have addressed. To evaluate the state
of lipogenesis and lipolysis in Alms1-/- mice with or without treatment, we intraperitoneally
injected 13C-labeled glucose (New Figure 4J-K and S4N). As compared to WT controls, in
Alms1-/- mice, we observed an increase in 13C-glycerol-3-phosphate and alterations in 13C-
glucose-6-phosphate in plasma, as well as lower retention of 13C-glycerol-3-phosphate and
accumulation of 13C-citrate in the liver, indicating a shift of glucose carbon toward lipid
synthesis. Upon neutralization of ACBP, these parameters largely return to normal, reflecting
the restoration of a normal glucose metabolism. We conclude that reducing excess ACBP
normalizes metabolism in Alms1-/- mice even without correcting the autophagy deficit.
Remark No. 3 by reviewer No. 1: Knock-down in primary hepatocytes: In their resubmitted
study, the authors have used primary hepatocytes to knock down acbp via siRNA to
demonstrate the intracellular effects of ACBP inhibition. This methodology, however, raises
concerns in light of their primary aim of investigating the extracellular role of ACBP. By
focusing on intracellular knockdown through siRNA in primary hepatocytes, the authors
introduce a mechanistic inconsistency, as this approach (primarily) targets intracellular ACBP,
which does not align with their hypothesis that extracellular ACBP is the critical driver of
metabolic disturbances.
Our response: We thank the reviewer for raising this important point. We fully agree that our
central hypothesis relates to the role of extracellular ACBP in the development of metabolic
disorders. The siRNA experiments in primary hepatocytes were not intended to contradict this
hypothesis, but rather to complement it by exploring whether ACBP has any intracellular
effects on hepatocytes. We recognize that this could be confusing and have clarified the
rationale and scope of these experiments in the revised manuscript.
To better address the reviewer's concern, we highlight that multiple independent studies have
shown that inhibition of the ACBP system, whether through extracellular neutralizing
3
antibodies, complete gene inactivation (eliminating both intracellular and extracellular ACBP),
or mutation of the ACBP receptor (selectively affecting extracellular signaling), consistently
produces comparable biological outcomes. These include protection against (i) liver damage
induced by methionine-choline deficient, (ii) hepatic steatosis induced by HFD, (iii) systemic
metabolic shifts induced by high-dose corticotherapy, and (iv) knee osteoarthritis induced by
mechanical destabilization. In our opinion, these findings strongly suggest that the inhibition
of extracellular Acbp with the antibody affects the system by on-target effects. Moreover, they
indicate that inhibition of extracellular Acbp (which is achieved by injection of the antibody or
by mutation of the receptor) is sufficient to obtain protection against obesogenic stimuli.
We have revised the Discussion section to better clarify the consistency across models and
approaches and to make our mechanistic interpretation more consistent with our central
hypothesis.

network analysis
First author: Yaiza Corral Nieto
Lead author: José Manuel Bravo-San Pedro
Re-submission date: 08/07/2025
General response to the reviewers
We would like to express our sincere gratitude to the four reviewers for their constructive
comments and suggestions during the three rounds of review. We were able to address and
respond to all of their questions during this process, and the changes and results we added have
allowed us to significantly improve the manuscript. We are convinced that these improvements
enhance the value and potential impact of our work.
Point-by-point reply to Reviewer No. 1.
Overall: While I appreciate the authors’ substantial efforts to strengthen their manuscript
through extensive multi-omics profiling and the addition of new experiments, I must raise two
essential issues that remain inadequately addressed and preclude my recommendation for
acceptance in the manuscript’s current form.
Conclusion: I remain positive about the general direction and novelty of the study. However,
until the two concerns outlined above — the underrepresentation of ACBP KO data and the
indirect nature of lipogenesis evidence — are appropriately addressed, I cannot recommend the
manuscript for publication. I encourage the authors to revise the manuscript to strengthen
mechanistic clarity while maintaining their otherwise thorough systems-level approach.
Remark No. 1 by reviewer No. 1: Misrepresentation of the ACBP KO Mouse Literature
The authors originally stated that ACBP knockout mice are non-viable, which has now been
corrected in their response. However, their revised justification for not using these mice —
namely that they only display transient metabolic phenotypes — is misleading. Multiple
published studies (e.g. PMID 28343864, 30938715 and 33346070) have demonstrated the
viability of ACBP knockout mice and described robust phenotypes, including enhanced energy
expenditure, WAT beiging, resistance to obesity, and improved glucose homeostasis. Given
this, I strongly urge the authors to acknowledge this body of work more transparently and revise
their discussion to reflect that viable ACBP KO models exist and are informative. While I
understand the challenges of generating a double KO (Alms1/Acbp), dismissing existing
models may diminish the credibility of the mechanistic claims made in the manuscript.
Our response: We sincerely thank the reviewer for this important comment and fully agree
with his/her observation. We appreciate the opportunity to correct and clarify this point. In
response to the reviewer's point, we have revised the discussion section to more transparently
1
acknowledge the existing body of literature on viable Acbp knockout mice and their relevance.
Specifically, we have expanded the limitations of our study to include the following statement:
“One major limitation of our study is the absence of a genetic ACBP knockout model. We
acknowledge that viable Acbp knockout mice exist and display robust phenotypes, including
enhanced energy expenditure, beiging of white adipose tissue, resistance to diet-induced
obesity, and improved glucose homeostasis, as reported in several studies (PMIDs 28343864,
30938715 and 33346070). These findings highlight the mechanistic relevance of the ACBP
system in energy metabolism and validate its role in obesity-related phenotypes. While these
models offer important insights, generating a double Alms1/Acbp knockout mouse model was
not technically feasible within the timeframe and scope of this study. Based on our experience
with conditional Acbp knockout strategies, we estimate that developing such a model, requiring
multiple breeding steps, tissue-specific alleles, and ethical approvals for animal
experimentation, would require at least 9-12 months. Nonetheless, our study incorporates in
vitro models using both primary hepatocytes and HepG2 cells, in which ALMS1 was genetically
silenced or knocked out, supporting the relevance of our findings at the cellular level. In
addition, prior studies have shown that inhibiting the ACBP system in vivo—whether by
neutralizing extracellular Acbp, knocking out the Dbi gene (thus removing both intra- and
extracellular ACBP), or mutating the ACBP receptor (thus affecting only signaling by
extracellular ACBP)—provides comparable protection against liver damage induced by
methionine-choline deficiency (PMID: 36191214), hepatic steatosis triggered by high-fat diets
(PMID: 35436993, 38582872), and high-dose corticotherapy-induced metabolic shifts leading
to visceral obesity, steatosis, dyslipidemia and insulin resistance (PMID: 39578649). These
findings strongly suggest that extracellular ACBP has pathogenic effects that can be
counteracted by neutralizing antibodies acting on target. Our study identified metabolites that
are dysregulated exclusively in the AöS model, but not in the DIO model, and are normalized
by ACBP inhibition. This suggests that ACBP neutralization could have wide-ranging benefits
across various models of metabolic dysfunction”.
We hope this expanded discussion adequately addresses the reviewer’s concern and reinforces
the scientific context and rationale for our experimental approach.
The authors use changes in 13C-glucose-derived glycerol-3-phosphate (G3P) as a proxy for
altered lipogenesis. However, G3P is primarily derived from glycolysis and reflects glycerol
backbone availability rather than fatty acid synthesis per se. This metabolite alone is not a
definitive readout of de novo lipogenesis. Without parallel measurement of 13C-incorporation
into fatty acid chains (e.g., palmitate or other lipids), the claim that ACBP neutralization
normalizes lipogenesis remains speculative. I encourage the authors to provide additional tracer
data that more directly quantifies lipid synthesis.
Our response:
We thank the reviewer for this scientifically sound comment. We fully agree that glycerol-3-
phosphate alone does not provide a direct proxy for de novo lipogenesis. Thanks to the
reviewer's suggestion, we expanded our analysis by incorporating additional 13C tracer data that
directly measure 13C incorporation from 13C-labeled glucose into palmitate in the liver, thus
providing stronger evidence of fatty acid synthesis. These new results have been included in
the revised manuscript (Figure 4J-K, Figure S4N-O, and Supplementary Table S6) and are
detailed in the Results section.
“Finally, we evaluated lipogenesis in Alms1⁻/⁻ mice by intraperitoneal administration of ¹³C-
labeled glucose (Figure S4N). In these obese animals, an increase in ¹³C-palmitate was
observed in the liver, indicating de novo lipogenesis from glucose (Figure 4J). In parallel, we
identified an uncoupling between plasma (increased) and hepatic (decreased) ¹³C-glycerol-3-
phosphate (gly3P) levels, suggesting accelerated consumption of this metabolite in the liver for
triglyceride synthesis. This pattern is consistent with a hyperactive lipogenic state in which
gly3P does not accumulate freely, but is rapidly channeled towards fatty acid esterification
(Figure S4O). Of note, treatment with anti-ACBP antibody prevented both ¹³C-palmitate
accumulation and ¹³C-gly3P uncoupling, indicating the normalization of carbon flux into lipid
pathways and a restoration of metabolic balance (Figures 4J and S4O). Moreover, a positive
correlation between the levels of ¹³C-labeled palmitate and body weight was observed (Figure
4K), supporting the idea that ACBP neutralization prevents obesity in Alms1-/- mice through an
effect on lipogenesis. In conclusion, ACBP neutralization normalizes lipid metabolism both in
isolated hepatocytes from Alms1-/- mice and in vivo, in mice with this genotype, even without
restoring impaired autophagy.”
These results fully support the initial hypothesis, confirming that neutralization of ACBP
reverses metabolic reprogramming towards accrued lipogenesis in Alms1⁻/⁻ mice.
Overall: The authors have addressed all my concerns. The inclusion of pre-obese, weight
matched Alsm1 knockout mice as the inclusion of weight matched DIO controls overcome all
concerns I had and I delighted to recommend publication of the paper.
Our response: No further action is required on our side with respect to Reviewer No. 2. We
thank reviewers 2, 3 and 4 for their contributions to this work.
